questions.stem: The controlling cue here is “Explain the value of pairing two dated condition reports. / Ask what a second date lets the team compare. / A before and after…”. Which option is consistent with it?

answer.exemplar: One report describes a moment, so it cannot show whether the object is improving or deteriorating. questions.learningObjective: Explain how reflectography reveals a hidden composition.

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about what infrared reflectography shows. the method records the layer below the paint, so an abandoned first composition remains legible. A marginal reminder adds: ask which layer the method records. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: The question turns on what the note above shows about what infrared reflectography shows. Given the proposal "Ask which layer the method records", which choice is consistent with the evidence in the passage?

answer.exemplar: Infrared reflectography sends light into the paint and records what comes back from the drawing layer beneath it, so lines of the earlier composition appear as darker marks under the visible picture. Where the painter changed his mind, the underdrawing keeps the first idea, and where he repeated a form, the underdrawing confirms the plan rather than the finished effect.

questions.explanation: The method records the layer below the paint, so an abandoned first composition remains legible. What it shows is the drawing, not the finished surface, which is why it differs from what the eye sees.
questions.hint: Ask which layer the method records.

answer.exemplar: An examination observes the object as it is: the layers, the colours, the fibres, the structure and the marks of use. A report may narrow the possible intentions, but it cannot read them off the surface as a laboratory result.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A before and after pair of reports
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a pair of reports beats a single report.

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about a before and after pair of reports. one report is a snapshot and a snapshot cannot show a direction. A marginal reminder adds: ask what a second date lets the reader see. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: The question turns on what the note above shows about a before and after pair of reports. Given the proposal "Ask what a second date lets the reader see", which choice is consistent with the evidence in the passage?

answer.exemplar: A single report fixes a state of the object at one date and therefore cannot show a direction of change. Two reports at known dates let the same entries be set against one another, and a stable adhesive in 1955 can be compared with a brittle one in 2005. The interval between them then becomes the measure, and the reader can see whether a treatment arrested a problem or only postponed it.

questions.explanation: One report is a snapshot and a snapshot cannot show a direction. Two dated reports make the same entries comparable, and the interval between them measures what changed and what did not.
questions.hint: Ask what a second date lets the reader see.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the two labels should be kept distinct.

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about the gap between circle of and after. the labels carry different claims about closeness in time and training, and merging them erases a distinction the catalogue exists to make. A marginal reminder adds: ask what each label claims about the work. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: A reviewer is weighing competing claims about the gap between circle of and after, among them "Ask what each label claims about the work". Based only on the excerpt above, which answer is the one the evidence warrants?

answer.exemplar: The two labels are not decorative phrases but statements about where the work stands in relation to the master. Circle of says that the followers worked in his presence, so the debt is direct and can often be traced in dated records. After his death says that the work belongs to the workshop tradition that continued without him. Merging them loses the historical difference that the catalogue is meant to preserve.

questions.explanation: The labels carry different claims about closeness in time and training, and merging them erases a distinction the catalogue exists to make. Smoothing the phrase away loses the work's position.
questions.hint: Ask what each label claims about the work.
